Workflow.description: A GitHub Actions workflow or action metadata file, with lint findings and run history.

action-deps.description: Each third-party action across every workflow that uses it: pinned to a commit SHA everywhere (D70, docs/design/github-actions-standards.md).
action-deps.rationale: A compromised action reaches every workflow that runs it, so in an incident the question is which workflows use it and at which refs. Scoring per action answers that and shows any use still unpinned; bronze is the only level because an action is either pinned everywhere or not.

pinned-everywhere.fix: Pin this action to a full commit SHA in every workflow that uses it. Resolve the tag with `git ls-remote https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> refs/tags/<tag>` and peel an annotated tag (`^{}`) so the SHA is the commit.
pinned-everywhere.rationale: One unpinned use is enough for a moved tag to run new code with that workflow's token, so an action counts as pinned only when every workflow pins it.

action-deps.title: Third-party actions pinned

ci-reliability.description: Whether green CI means good on the default branch: failures visible and counted, including those a re-run hid, every job bounded by a timeout, and a branch that rarely fails (D70; docs/design/thresholds.md for the tiers). Speed is ci-speed.
ci-reliability.rationale: CI is only worth running if red means something broke and green means nothing did; flaky, hidden or hung jobs teach people to ignore it. Bronze makes failures visible and bounded and keeps the branch out of long red streaks; silver and gold each halve the share of first-try failures a reader must check, over enough runs to tell the tiers apart.

every-job-has-timeout.fix: Set `timeout-minutes` on every job; the default is 360 minutes of a hung runner.
every-job-has-timeout.rationale: Without `timeout-minutes` a hung job holds a runner for GitHub's default of 360 minutes before it fails, spending runner time and delaying the signal everyone is waiting for.

fail-rate-under-10.fix: Open the failed runs in the evidence and classify each cause: a flaky test (fix or quarantine it in its test file), infrastructure (pin or retry the step in the workflow file), or real breakage merged to the branch (add the missing check to the pull request workflow).
fail-rate-under-10.rationale: At silver, failures are rare enough that each can be classified as a flake, infrastructure or a break a pull request check missed. It needs a minimum number of runs, because with few runs one failure moves the rate across tiers.

fail-rate-under-20.fix: Open the failed runs in the evidence, find the failing jobs, and fix their causes in the code or the workflow file. The rate is over the last runs on the branch, so it falls as passing runs replace failed ones. Re-running a failure doesn't help: a run that passed on a later attempt counts as failed, continue-on-error, `|| true` and skips on the default branch are caught by failures-visible, and cancelled runs are shown here.
fail-rate-under-20.rationale: Every red run costs someone a look, and a re-run that turns it green hides a flaky test or step; counting first-try failures stops re-runs from lowering the rate. Bronze is the first step for a branch that fails often.

fail-rate-under-5.fix: Open each failed run in the evidence and fix its cause where it lives (the test, the workflow file, or the check the pull request lacked), so that every failure on the branch is rare enough to be looked at.
fail-rate-under-5.rationale: At gold, a red run on the default branch is rare enough that every one is looked at and fixed at its cause, so red keeps its meaning.

failures-visible.fix: For each listed job or step in the workflow file: remove `continue-on-error`, `|| true` (or `set +e`), or the `if:` that skips it on the default branch. If a step is expected to fail, give it an `id:` and check `steps.<id>.outcome` in a later step, so the failure is still asserted.
failures-visible.rationale: `continue-on-error`, `|| true`, `set +e` and a skip on the default branch each turn a failure into a pass, so the fail-rate rules would count it green. It is their prerequisite, so it sits at bronze.

main-not-stuck-red.fix: Fix the default branch before anything else: open the failed runs in the evidence, find the failing job, and fix its cause in the code or in the workflow file under .github/workflows/.
main-not-stuck-red.rationale: A default branch that keeps failing breaks everyone who branches from it, and each new failure hides behind the last. Three in a row means the break is not being fixed.

still-running.fix: Re-enable the workflow (`gh workflow enable <file>`, or the Actions tab), or delete its file from .github/workflows/ if it is retired.
still-running.rationale: A disabled workflow's old run history still reads green, so it would pass every run-history rule while checking nothing. GitHub disables scheduled workflows in a public repository after 60 days without activity, and anyone can disable one by hand. A workflow whose triggers simply stop matching stays active and is not caught here.

ci-reliability.title: CI reliability

ci-security.description: What an attacker could do through a workflow: pinned actions, least- privilege tokens, no risky triggers with write access, and zizmor and actionlint clean (D70, docs/design/github-actions-standards.md).
ci-security.rationale: A workflow runs with the repository's token and secrets, so a hijacked action, an injected expression or an over-broad token is a route to pushing code or stealing credentials. Bronze closes the direct routes, silver removes write access where untrusted events arrive, and gold leaves nothing zizmor flags unexplained.

actionlint-clean.fix: Fix what actionlint reports (`actionlint` in the repository root).
actionlint-clean.rationale: A syntax error, a mistyped expression or a wrong action input only shows up when the workflow runs, and actionlint also finds script injection; catching these in the file is cheaper than a broken run.

least-privilege-token.fix: Declare `permissions:` at the top of the workflow (read-only, e.g. `contents: read`) and grant writes per job.
least-privilege-token.rationale: A job without `permissions:` gets the token's default scopes, which can include write access, so any compromised step can push code or change releases. Read-only by default limits what one bad step can do.

no-high-findings.fix: Fix zizmor's high-severity findings (`zizmor --offline .github/workflows actions`); see https://docs.zizmor.sh/audits/.
no-high-findings.rationale: zizmor's high-severity audits, such as template injection and dangerous triggers, find ways for untrusted input to run code with the workflow's token. One is enough for an attacker, so they belong in the floor.

no-medium-findings.fix: Fix zizmor's medium findings (e.g. `artipacked`: set `persist-credentials: false` on checkout).
no-medium-findings.rationale: Medium findings widen what one compromised step can reach: a checkout token left in `.git/config`, for example, is readable by every later step and by any artifact that uploads the directory.

no-write-tokens-on-risky-triggers.fix: Don't combine pull_request_target/workflow_run/issue_comment with write permissions; split privileged steps into a separate workflow.
no-write-tokens-on-risky-triggers.rationale: These triggers run in the base repository's context on events outsiders can cause, such as a fork's pull request or a comment, so a write token there puts a privileged credential within reach of untrusted input.

pinned-to-sha.fix: Pin every third-party `uses:` to a full commit SHA. Resolve the tag with `git ls-remote https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> refs/tags/<tag>` and peel an annotated tag (`^{}`) so the SHA is the commit, then put the tag in a comment. Let Dependabot update them.
pinned-to-sha.rationale: A tag or branch can be moved to new code after review, and that code runs with the workflow's token and secrets; only a commit SHA fixes what runs.

zizmor-clean.fix: Resolve or explicitly ignore (with a reason) zizmor's low and informational findings.
zizmor-clean.rationale: Low and informational findings are weak signals one by one, but each fixed or ignored with a written reason lets a reviewer tell a known trade-off from an oversight. That is polish beyond the direct risks, so it is gold.

ci-security.title: CI security

ci-speed.description: Whether CI answers quickly and spends no runner time on superseded commits: a cost and feedback-time concern, separate from whether CI can be trusted (ci-reliability; docs/design/thresholds.md).
ci-speed.rationale: Slow runs and runs for superseded commits cost runner minutes and queue time, and make people wait or switch task for feedback. Speed is not a correctness or security property, so it has its own card rather than holding a reliable workflow back.

cancels-superseded-runs.fix:
Add, at the top of the workflow file:
  concurrency:
    group: "${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}"
    cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
A new push to a pull request then cancels its old run, while every
run on main still finishes.
cancels-superseded-runs.rationale: Without a concurrency group per ref, each push to a pull request starts a new run while the old one, whose result no longer matters, keeps a runner busy.

fast-feedback.fix: Keep the p90 run under 15 minutes: split slow jobs, cache builds, move long suites off the PR path.
fast-feedback.rationale: Past the bound, developers switch to other work while they wait and come back late to a failure. The bound is a chosen point, not a measured one.

ci-speed.title: CI speed

docs.description: Each Markdown document in this repository: links that resolve.
docs.rationale: Markdown docs are how a repository explains itself to people and agents. Resolving links can be checked in any repository with no build or network, so that is where the starter begins.

links-resolve.fix: Fix or remove the relative links in the evidence.
links-resolve.rationale: Moving or renaming a file breaks the links to it without failing any build; the reader finds out by following a dead link.

docs.title: Docs with working links

go-file-size.description: Files with more than 800 lines violate. The measure is the lines over the limit, so a violating file that grows is a regression and one that shrinks is an improvement.
go-file-size.rationale: A file has to fit in a reader's head, or an agent's context window, to be changed safely, and long files are where review gets skimmed. A line limit is a crude proxy, but it is cheap to measure and moves the right way: the ratchet stops growth while existing files are split.

within-limit.fix: Move code out of this file into new modules until it is within the limit. Do not add new functionality to it.
within-limit.rationale: A file over the limit gets harder to review with every line added. Measuring the lines over the limit makes each split count as progress and each addition a regression.

go-file-size.title: Go files within 800 lines

go-panics.description: Each match of the pattern is a violation. The measure is the number of matches, so a file that gains one is a regression and one that loses one is an improvement.
go-panics.rationale: Some code patterns are known to cause trouble in a codebase: a deprecated call, a debug print, an unchecked unwrap. Counting them per file turns a convention reviewers would otherwise have to remember into a check that stops new ones and tracks the old ones to zero.

no-matches.fix: Return an error instead; a panic in a request path takes the server down.
no-matches.rationale: Each match is a place the convention is broken. A new one is cheapest to avoid in the change that adds it, and the count shows the old ones going down.

go-panics.title: No panics outside tests

go-staticcheck.description: Every file staticcheck checks is clean. The measure is its findings, so a new finding is a regression and a fixed one an improvement; a new file must arrive clean.
go-staticcheck.rationale: A tool's findings help only if new ones can't pile up unnoticed. The tool keeps its own rules and configuration, so its findings match a run outside the portal; the portal adds one level, clean, and a ratchet that blocks new findings while existing ones are paid down.

no-findings.fix: Fix the tool's findings (the record's command reruns them), or configure the rule in the tool's own config file with a comment saying why.
no-findings.rationale: Each finding is a defect or a risk as the tool's authors define it, and it is cheapest to fix in the change that introduces it, while its author still has the context.

go-staticcheck.title: No staticcheck findings

openfga-openssf.description: OpenSSF Scorecard's checks, as Scorecard scores them. Its one level, ten, means a check scores 10 out of 10. The box adds only the ratchet: a check's gap to 10 is the measure, so a score that drops fails a pull request and one that rises is an improvement. A check Scorecard adds in a new release doesn't fail the gate.
openfga-openssf.rationale: OpenSSF Scorecard is an established, openly governed standard for supply-chain security, so the portal carries its checks as OpenSSF defines them rather than writing weaker copies that would compete with it. Its one level is Scorecard's own maximum, and the ratchet stops any check from falling while the gap is paid down.

ten.fix: Follow the check's documentation (in the evidence). The check, its scoring and its remediation are OpenSSF's.
ten.rationale: Each point below 10 is a supply-chain weakness OpenSSF documents with its risk and remediation; holding every check at its current score keeps a regression from slipping in unnoticed.

openfga-openssf.title: OpenSSF Scorecard

repo-hygiene.description: This repository's basics: a README and CODEOWNERS, then a catch-all owner, owners that are teams and a licence.
repo-hygiene.rationale: These files tell a newcomer or an agent what the repository is, who reviews changes to it, and whether its code may be reused, and they can be checked in any repository with no build or network. Bronze is a README and a CODEOWNERS file; silver makes ownership complete and unambiguous and adds a licence.

codeowners-catch-all.fix: Start CODEOWNERS with a `*` rule so every path has an owner.
codeowners-catch-all.rationale: A path no rule matches has no owner, so changes to it get no automatic reviewer. A leading catch-all gives every path a default that later, more specific rules override.

has-codeowners.fix: Add .github/CODEOWNERS so changes are routed to an owning team.
has-codeowners.rationale: Without CODEOWNERS, GitHub requests no reviewer for a pull request and nothing in the repository says who owns the code.

has-license.fix: Add a LICENSE file (or a note in the README if the code is internal-only).
has-license.rationale: Without a licence, default copyright applies and nobody else may legally use, change or share the code, even in a public repository.

has-readme.fix: Add a README of at least 50 words: what this is, how to run it, who owns it.
has-readme.rationale: The README is the first thing a person or an agent reads to learn what a repository is and how to run it; without one they reverse-engineer it from the code.

owners-are-teams.fix: Name teams (@org/team), or for a single-maintainer repository only personal handles (@user). Do not mix teams with individuals, and do not use emails.
owners-are-teams.rationale: A team keeps ownership when people leave; a mix of teams and individuals, or an email, leaves it unclear who answers for the code. All-personal handles are accepted so a single-maintainer repository can reach silver.

repo-hygiene.title: Repository basics

vs-spicedb-ecosystem.description: Contributors, release cadence, SDKs and governance.
vs-spicedb-ecosystem.rationale: A team adopting an authorization server depends on it for years, so who maintains it, how often it ships and in which languages it can be called matter as much as how it runs today.

contributors.fix: Lower the barrier to a first contribution.
contributors.rationale: More contributors spread the bus factor and the review load.

foundation.fix: Move governance to a neutral foundation.
foundation.rationale: Neutral governance means no single vendor can relicense or abandon the project the team depends on.

official-sdks.fix: Maintain a client for another major language.
official-sdks.rationale: Every service that asks for a decision needs a client in its own language, and an unofficial one may lag the API.

release-cadence.rationale: Frequent releases ship security fixes to users without long waits or backports.

vs-spicedb-ecosystem.title: Ecosystem

vs-spicedb-footprint.description: The binary on disk and resident memory, idle and loaded.
vs-spicedb-footprint.rationale: Authorization servers run as a sidecar or a small fleet next to every service, so their size and memory are paid many times over.

binary-size.fix: Trim dependencies compiled into the server.
binary-size.rationale: The binary is pulled by every node that schedules a replica, so its size is paid on every cold start.

idle-memory.rationale: Idle memory is the cost of every replica that is not busy, which is most of them outside peak hours.

loaded-memory.fix: Profile the heap under load, including caches.
loaded-memory.rationale: Memory under load sets the container limit; past it the replica is killed, and every check it was answering fails.

vs-spicedb-footprint.title: Footprint

vs-spicedb-modelling.description: What a team can express and ask, each fact cited from the docs or source at the pinned release, or probed against the server.
vs-spicedb-modelling.rationale: A model the server cannot express ends up in application code, where it is checked inconsistently and cannot be audited in one place.

change-feed.fix: Expose relationship changes from a position, by stream or by page.
change-feed.rationale: Search indexes and caches that filter by permission need to follow changes instead of re-reading everything.

conditions.fix: Support conditions on relationships evaluated against request context.
conditions.rationale: Time windows, IP ranges and resource attributes are part of many access rules, and without conditions they move into application code.

consistency-tokens.fix: Return a token from each write that a read can require, as Zanzibar's zookies do.
consistency-tokens.rationale: Without it, a check just after a revoke can still be answered from a stale cache or replica: the new-enemy problem the Zanzibar paper describes.

contextual-tuples.fix: Accept request-scoped relationships on check and list calls.
contextual-tuples.rationale: Facts the caller already knows, like the user's current organisation, can then be used without being written and kept in sync.

exclusion.fix: Support exclusion and intersection operators in the model.
exclusion.rationale: Blocks, suspensions and "member and verified" rules need subtraction and intersection, not only unions.

list-users.fix: Add an API that lists the subjects holding a permission.
list-users.rationale: "Who can see this?" is the question an access review or a sharing dialog asks, and it cannot be answered by checks alone.

model-tests.fix: Run assertion files about a model from the CLI, in CI.
model-tests.rationale: A model change can grant access nobody intended, and assertions in CI catch it before it ships.

multi-tenant.fix: Let one server hold isolated models and relationships per tenant.
multi-tenant.rationale: Without it, each tenant or environment needs its own deployment, or tenants share a model and must be kept apart by naming alone.

wildcards.fix: Support a relationship to every subject of a type.
wildcards.rationale: Public resources would otherwise need one relationship per user, which grows with the user base and misses new users.

vs-spicedb-modelling.title: Modelling

vs-spicedb-operability.description: Metrics, traces, protocols, datastores and migrations, as shipped.
vs-spicedb-operability.rationale: The team that runs the server needs to see it, reach it and upgrade it without writing glue around it.

datastores.rationale: A team can then run the server on a database it already operates, instead of adopting one for authorization alone.

http-by-default.fix: Serve HTTP/JSON next to gRPC in the default configuration.
http-by-default.rationale: Shell scripts, browsers and languages without a gRPC client can call an HTTP API without generated code.

migrate-command.fix: Ship a migrate command in the server binary.
migrate-command.rationale: Upgrades then need only the new binary, not a separate migration tool pinned to the right version.

otel-tracing.rationale: A trace shows which part of a slow request was the authorization check, across services.

prometheus-metrics.rationale: Latency and error metrics are how the operator learns about a slow or failing server before its callers do.

vs-spicedb-operability.title: Operability

vs-spicedb-performance.description: Start, write, check and list on a 33k-relationship corpus, memory datastore, each product's gRPC API at 16 workers.
vs-spicedb-performance.rationale: An authorization server sits on the request path of every service that asks it, so its check tail is added to theirs, and its start time bounds how fast a rescheduled replica serves again.

check-latency.fix: Profile check resolution and its cache, then rerun the harness.
check-latency.rationale: A page or API call often makes several checks, so the per-check tail becomes the caller's typical latency.

check-throughput.fix: Profile check resolution under load, then rerun the harness.
check-throughput.rationale: Checks per second on one machine decide how many replicas a given request rate needs.

list-latency.fix: Profile ListObjects or LookupResources, then rerun the harness.
list-latency.rationale: Search results and list pages filter by what the user can see, and a slow reverse lookup forces callers to check each item instead.

ready.fix: Profile server start, then rerun the harness.
ready.rationale: A replica that is not ready cannot answer checks, so start time is the floor on recovery after a crash, a deploy or a scale-out.

write-throughput.fix: Profile the write path, then rerun the harness.
write-throughput.rationale: Every grant, share and group change is a write, and a slow backfill holds up a migration onto the server.

vs-spicedb-performance.title: Performance

vs-spicedb-supply-chain.description: What the release binary pulls in and what a user can verify about it.
vs-spicedb-supply-chain.rationale: An authorization server decides who may do what, so a compromised or vulnerable build compromises every service that trusts it.

go-modules.fix: Remove or replace dependencies the server does not need.
go-modules.rationale: Each module is code from another maintainer that runs with the server's privileges and has to be watched for advisories.

known-vulns.fix: Upgrade the affected modules and release.
known-vulns.rationale: govulncheck reports only vulnerable code the binary can call, so each finding is reachable rather than a lockfile match.

provenance.fix: Publish signed SLSA provenance with each release.
provenance.rationale: Provenance lets a user verify that the archive was built from the tagged source by the project's CI, not by whoever uploaded it.

sbom.fix: Publish an SBOM with each release.
sbom.rationale: An SBOM lets a user find out whether a new advisory affects the version they run without rebuilding it.

vs-spicedb-supply-chain.title: Supply chain

vs-spicedb.description: OpenFGA v1.23.0 against SpiceDB v1.57.1, both on the memory datastore and each product's gRPC API, on one VM: timed factors are medians of 5 scripted runs over a 33k-relationship corpus, and yes/no facts cite the docs or source at the pinned release. The benchmark is Toolbox's: its maintainers chose the factors and set every bar before the run. Not covered: Postgres or MySQL datastores, more than one node, sustained load over hours, or any other release.
vs-spicedb.title: Against SpiceDB
